Chapter 1: Introduction & Literature Survey

1.1 Problem Background

The continuous growth of wireless multimedia services, satellite imaging, autonomous robotics, and remote telemetry has placed unprecedented demands on the physical layer of digital communication systems. In visual communication networks, transmission involves serializing dense two-dimensional image matrices into binary data streams and transmitting them across band-limited, noisy channels. During propagation, radio frequency (RF) signals are corrupted by thermal agitation and background radiation, universally characterized as Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN).

Digital modulation schemes dictate how information bits are mapped into analog baseband waveforms. The fundamental engineering challenge is governed by Shannon's channel capacity theorem:

$$C = B \log_2 \left(1 + rac{S}{N} ight) \quad [ ext{bits/second}]$$

Designers must balance two competing objectives: spectral efficiency (transmitting maximum bits per second per Hertz, η = Rb/B) and energy efficiency (minimizing the required bit energy-to-noise ratio, Eb/N0, to attain a specified bit error probability). Binary Phase Shift Keying (BPSK) provides high noise immunity by allocating 1 bit per symbol with maximum antipodal Euclidean distance, but requires significant bandwidth (η = 1 bps/Hz). Conversely, 16-ary Quadrature Amplitude Modulation (16-QAM) quadruples spectral efficiency (η = 4 bps/Hz) by simultaneously modulating amplitude and phase; however, it reduces the distance between adjacent constellation points, increasing susceptibility to channel noise.

1.3 Problem Statement

To formulate, model, and simulate an end-to-end digital image communication transceiver system in MATLAB that serializes digital images into binary bitstreams, executes dual-path BPSK and 16-QAM baseband modulation with exact Gray coding and unit energy normalization, transmits signals through a calibrated AWGN channel, performs coherent maximum-likelihood demodulation, reconstructs received images, and rigorously quantifies the trade-off between spectral efficiency and noise sensitivity across physical and perceptual metrics.

1.4 Project Objectives

  1. End-to-End Transceiver Modeling: Construct a modular MATLAB simulation pipeline encompassing image ingestion, 8-bit MSB serialization, digital modulation, AWGN channel emulation, coherent demodulation, and spatial image reconstruction.
  2. Spectral Efficiency vs. Noise Sensitivity Trade-off: Empirically demonstrate that 16-QAM achieves a 4x throughput enhancement (reducing channel symbols from 524,288 to 131,072 for a 256x256 image) while incurring an anticipated ~4.2 dB SNR penalty compared to BPSK.
  3. Theoretical Analytical Verification: Validate Monte Carlo simulated BER curves against theoretical closed-form bounds (Q-function for BPSK and Craig's Gray-coded formula for 16-QAM).
  4. Perceptual Image Quality Assessment: Evaluate visual degradation using Mean Squared Error (MSE), Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), and Structural Similarity Index (SSIM).
  5. Phase-Space Constellation Scattering: Map In-Phase (I) and Quadrature (Q) signal clouds across SNR levels to observe decision boundary crossings.
  6. Advanced Extensions Prototyping: Implement (7,4) Hamming Forward Error Correction (FEC), flat Rayleigh fading with MMSE equalization, and an Adaptive Modulation and Coding (AMC) policy.
  7. Interactive GUI Development: Construct an interactive application (dcs_gui.m) facilitating live interactive demonstrations and testing.

Chapter 2: Conceptual Framework & Methodology

2.1 Complex Engineering Problem Formulation

In digital image transmission, the physical channel is characterized by finite bandwidth B and thermal noise power spectral density N0. The design problem requires simultaneously satisfying:

  • Bandwidth Constraints: Minimizing channel occupation time Ttrans = Ns / Rs, where Ns is the total channel symbols and Rs is the symbol rate.
  • Bit-to-Symbol Constellation Spacing: For an average symbol power Es = 1, higher-order constellations pack more points into the 2D complex plane. The minimum Euclidean distance between neighboring points shrinks, increasing the probability that noise vectors displace symbols across decision boundaries.
  • Non-Uniform Visual Impact of Bit Errors: Uncompressed digital images encode pixel luminance in 8-bit bytes (b7b6...b0). An error in the Most Significant Bit (b7, weight 128) alters luminance drastically (|ΔI| ≥ 128), whereas an error in the Least Significant Bit (b0, weight 1) is virtually imperceptible (|ΔI| = 1).

2.2 System Architecture & Block Diagram

The complete system architecture is organized into three core stages: Transmitter, AWGN Channel, and Receiver, supported by dual evaluation engines:

[Source Image: 256x256 px] ---> [Image to Binary Serialization (524,288 bits)] | +--------------------+--------------------+ | | v v [Path A: BPSK Modulator] [Path B: 16-QAM Modulator] [s = 1 - 2b, 1 bit/sym] [Gray 4-bit Grid, Es = 1] | | +--------------------+--------------------+ | v [AWGN Channel Model: r = s + w, w ~ CN(0, N0)] [Calibrated for Eb/No sweeps from 0 to 14 dB] | +--------------------+--------------------+ | | v v [Path A: BPSK Demodulator] [Path B: 16-QAM Demodulator] [Coherent Real-Axis Slicer] [Min Euclidean Distance Slicer] | | +--------------------+--------------------+ | v [Binary to Image Reconstruction (256x256 uint8)] | v +-----------------------------------+-----------------------------------+ | | v v [Signal Constellation Analysis] [Perceptual & BER Analysis Engine] - I/Q Scatter Clouds at 2, 6, 10, 14 dB - Semi-log BER vs Eb/No Curves - Decision Boundary Overlay - PSNR & SSIM Perception Curves - Voronoi Cell Dispersion Mapping - Spatial Pixel Error Heatmaps

2.3 Mathematical Modeling of Modulation Schemes

2.3.1 BPSK Modulation and Demodulation

In BPSK, each bit bi ∈ {0, 1} modulates the carrier phase by 0 or π radians. The complex baseband representation is:

$$s_i = (1 - 2b_i) \in \{+1, -1\}$$

Each symbol carries k = 1 bit. The average symbol energy is Es = Eb = 1, and the Euclidean distance is dmin, BPSK = |1 - (-1)| = 2.0. Under coherent detection, the received symbol ri = si + wi is demodulated via sign slicing:

$$\hat{b}_i = egin{cases} 0, & ext{if } \operatorname{Re}(r_i) \ge 0 \ 1, & ext{if } \operatorname{Re}(r_i) < 0 \end{cases}$$

The exact theoretical bit error probability over an AWGN channel is:

$$P_{b, ext{BPSK}} = Q\left(\sqrt{ rac{2E_b}{N_0}} ight) = rac{1}{2} \operatorname{erfc}\left(\sqrt{ rac{E_b}{N_0}} ight)$$

2.3.2 16-QAM Modulation and Gray Mapping

16-QAM encodes k = log2(16) = 4 bits per symbol. A 4-bit word [b1, b2, b3, b4] is split into In-Phase (I) and Quadrature (Q) PAM components:

$$ ext{Gray Mapping: } 00 o -3, \quad 01 o -1, \quad 11 o +1, \quad 10 o +3$$

The unnormalized symbol is sraw = Im + j Qm with average power:

$$E_{ ext{avg}} = rac{2(M - 1)}{3} = rac{2(16 - 1)}{3} = 10$$

To ensure unity average energy (Es = 1), symbols are scaled by 1/√10:

$$s = rac{I_m + j Q_m}{\sqrt{10}} \implies E_s = 1, \quad E_b = rac{E_s}{k} = rac{1}{4}$$

The minimum Euclidean distance between adjacent points in normalized 16-QAM is:

$$d_{\min, ext{16-QAM}} = rac{2}{\sqrt{10}} pprox 0.6325$$

The ratio of Euclidean distances demonstrates why 16-QAM is more sensitive to noise:

$$ rac{d_{\min, ext{BPSK}}}{d_{\min, ext{16-QAM}}} = rac{2.0}{0.6325} = \sqrt{10} pprox 3.162 \quad (pprox 10 ext{ dB in power ratio})$$

The exact theoretical bit error probability for Gray-coded 16-QAM is:

$$P_{b, ext{16-QAM}} pprox rac{4}{k} \left(1 - rac{1}{\sqrt{M}} ight) Q\left(\sqrt{ rac{3k}{M - 1} rac{E_b}{N_0}} ight) = rac{3}{4} Q\left(\sqrt{ rac{4}{5} rac{E_b}{N_0}} ight)$$

2.4 AWGN Channel Noise Calibration (Eb/N0 vs. Es/N0)

To ensure equitable benchmarking, channel noise is calibrated against energy per bit (Eb/N0) rather than energy per symbol (Es/N0):

$$ rac{E_s}{N_0} = k \cdot rac{E_b}{N_0} \implies \left( rac{E_s}{N_0} ight)_{ ext{dB}} = \left( rac{E_b}{N_0} ight)_{ ext{dB}} + 10 \log_{10}(k)$$

For normalized symbols (Es = 1), the noise power spectral density N0 and per-dimension Gaussian noise standard deviation σ are:

$$N_0 = rac{1}{k \cdot 10^{(E_b/N_0)_{ ext{dB}} / 10}}, \quad \sigma = \sqrt{ rac{N_0}{2}} = rac{1}{\sqrt{2k \cdot 10^{(E_b/N_0)_{ ext{dB}} / 10}}}$$

The complex noisy channel output is:

$$r = s + \sigma (n_I + j n_Q), \quad n_I, n_Q \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$$

2.5 Quantitative Performance Metrics

  • Bit Error Rate (BER): $ ext{BER} = rac{1}{N_{ ext{bits}}} \sum |b_i - \hat{b}_i|$
  • Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR): $ ext{PSNR} = 10 \log_{10}\left( rac{255^2}{ ext{MSE}} ight) ext{ dB}$, where $ ext{MSE} = rac{1}{HW}\sum (I_{ ext{orig}} - I_{ ext{rec}})^2$.
  • Structural Similarity Index (SSIM): Evaluates luminance, contrast, and structure preservation.
  • Spectral Efficiency (η): η = log2(M) bps/Hz.

Chapter 3: Innovation & Feasible Solution

3.1 Novel Aspects of the Proposed Framework

  1. Unified Physical-to-Perceptual Evaluation: Conventional communication models examine only BER curves. Our work links physical constellation dispersion directly to spatial pixel corruption and perceptual visual fidelity (PSNR/SSIM).
  2. Spatial Error Heatmap Generator: By isolating pixel intensity deltas |Iorig(x,y) - Irec(x,y)|, our framework visualizes the spatial clustering of bit errors, confirming that channel noise induces independent, identically distributed salt-and-pepper noise.
  3. Interactive Standalone GUI (dcs_gui.m): Developed an interactive MATLAB app featuring real-time sliders for Eb/N0, dynamic modulation switching, live I/Q constellation rendering, and instant metric readouts.
  4. Comprehensive Advanced Extensions (dcs_extensions.m): Built working prototypes for (7,4) Hamming Forward Error Correction, flat Rayleigh fading with MMSE equalization, and Adaptive Modulation and Coding (AMC) that dynamically switches between BPSK and 16-QAM based on channel SNR thresholds.

3.2 Technical & Economic Feasibility

  • Computational Feasibility: The transceiver architecture is vectorized for high computational efficiency. Simulating over 13 million bits across 13 SNR steps executes in under 20 seconds in MATLAB.
  • Hardware Implementation Feasibility: Both BPSK and 16-QAM algorithms can be readily deployed to low-cost Software-Defined Radios (such as RTL-SDR, HackRF, or ADALM-PLUTO) using open-source toolchains.
  • Economic Spectrum Savings: 16-QAM's 4x spectral efficiency quadruples user capacity within existing RF spectrum allocations, delivering substantial capital and operational expenditure savings for network operators.

3.3 Operational Constraints, Hardware Translation & Safety

  • Peak-to-Average Power Ratio (PAPR): BPSK maintains a constant envelope (PAPR = 0 dB), allowing Power Amplifiers (PAs) to operate near saturation for maximum efficiency. In contrast, 16-QAM has multiple amplitude levels (PAPR ≈ 2.55 dB), requiring amplifier power back-off to prevent non-linear distortion.
  • Carrier Synchronization & Phase Jitter: 16-QAM requires tight phase tracking; a phase error exceeding 5° causes rotational misclassification across constellation decision boundaries.
  • Radio Frequency Exposure & Green Communications: Operating at lower Eb/N0 thresholds reduces total RF radiated power, aligning with electromagnetic radiation safety limits (ICNIRP guidelines).

4.2 Visual Image Degradation Analysis

Figure 4.1: Side-by-side visual image reconstruction matrix comparing BPSK and 16-QAM across 2, 6, 10, and 14 dB.

Analysis: At 2 dB, both schemes show severe visual corruption. By 6 dB, BPSK reaches an acceptable visual quality threshold (PSNR = 30.79 dB, SSIM = 0.877), while 16-QAM remains degraded (PSNR = 22.13 dB). At 10 dB, BPSK achieves zero bit errors across all 524,288 bits, while 16-QAM achieves transparent quality (PSNR = 34.75 dB, SSIM = 0.938).

4.3 Signal Constellation Scattering & Phase-Space Analysis

Figure 4.2: In-Phase vs. Quadrature constellation scatter diagrams with decision boundaries.

Analysis: The scatter plots illustrate why 16-QAM is more sensitive to noise. The distance between adjacent points in 16-QAM is Δd = 2/√10 ≈ 0.6325, compared to Δd = 2.0 in BPSK. At 2 dB, 16-QAM noise clouds overlap across decision boundaries, causing high symbol error rates. Above 10 dB, the 16 clusters isolate cleanly into their respective decision regions.

4.4 Bit Error Rate (BER) vs. Eb/N0: Simulated vs. Theoretical Benchmark

Figure 4.3: Semi-logarithmic BER vs. Eb/N0 curves comparing Monte Carlo simulations against theoretical formulas.

Analysis: The simulated BER curves match theoretical formulas across the entire evaluation range. To achieve BER = 10-3, BPSK requires Eb/N0 ≈ 6.8 dB, whereas 16-QAM requires Eb/N0 ≈ 11.0 dB. This empirically confirms the 4.2 dB SNR trade-off penalty required by 16-QAM to deliver 4x higher spectral efficiency.

4.5 Perceptual Image Quality Analysis (PSNR and SSIM)

Figure 4.4: Objective perceptual metrics (PSNR and SSIM) plotted against channel Eb/N0.

Analysis: Both PSNR and SSIM exhibit a distinct "cliff effect" or threshold behavior. For BPSK, visual quality transitions sharply between 3 dB and 6 dB. For 16-QAM, this transition shifts rightward to between 7 dB and 10 dB.

4.6 Spatial Pixel Error & Bit-Flip Mapping

Figure 4.5: Spatial pixel error difference heatmaps (|Iorig - Irec|) at Eb/N0 = 6 dB.

Analysis: The error heatmaps confirm that channel noise induces independent, randomly distributed pixel errors. At 6 dB, BPSK exhibits only sparse, isolated errors, whereas 16-QAM exhibits widespread pixel errors across the entire image frame.

4.7 Advanced Extensions Prototype (Hamming FEC, Rayleigh Fading, AMC)

Figure 4.6: Advanced extensions prototype: (7,4) Hamming FEC, Rayleigh fading with MMSE, and Adaptive AMC.
Key Extension Findings:
  • Forward Error Correction (FEC): Systematic (7,4) Hamming coding reduces BPSK BER at 4 dB from 1.23 × 10-2 to 1.30 × 10-3, raising image PSNR from 23.93 dB to 33.51 dB (a coding gain of nearly 10 dB).
  • Rayleigh Multipath Fading: Multipath deep fades degrade uncoded 16-QAM even at 14 dB (BER = 1.97 × 10-2, PSNR = 22.96 dB), demonstrating the necessity of diversity techniques or equalization in practical wireless channels.
  • Adaptive Modulation and Coding (AMC): Dynamically switches from BPSK at low SNR (4 dB) to 16-QAM at high SNR (12 dB), achieving both link reliability and 4x data throughput.

Chapter 5: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) & Societal Impact

5.1 Alignment with UN Sustainable Development Goals

The project directly addresses four United Nations Sustainable Development Goals:

  • SDG 9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure (Target 9.c): 16-QAM's 4 bps/Hz spectral efficiency supports the rollout of high-capacity wireless backhaul and 5G/6G visual data networks.
  • SDG 7: Affordable and Clean Energy (Target 7.3): Cellular base stations account for significant global electricity consumption. Quantifying the 4.2 dB power trade-off enables dynamic power scaling and green transceiver operation.
  • SDG 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities (Target 11.5): BPSK's robustness provides a vital fallback mode for disaster reconnaissance drone feeds and emergency remote imaging during network outages.
  • SDG 12: Responsible Consumption and Production (Target 12.2): By quadrupling spectral efficiency, 16-QAM promotes efficient utilization of the finite radio frequency spectrum.

5.2 Direct Societal and Industrial Benefits

  • Remote Healthcare & Telemedicine: Enables reliable wireless transmission of diagnostic medical images (ultrasound, X-rays) to remote clinics without diagnostic loss.
  • Affordable Connectivity: Enhancing bits per Hertz reduces infrastructure costs per gigabyte, supporting affordable broadband expansion in underserved areas.

Chapter 6: Conclusion & References

6.1 Summary of Project Achievements

This project successfully designed, modeled, and simulated an end-to-end digital image communication system in MATLAB comparing BPSK and 16-QAM over AWGN channels. Key findings confirm that 16-QAM reduces channel transmission symbols by 75% (131,072 vs. 524,288 symbols for a 256x256 image) while incurring an expected ~4.2 dB SNR penalty due to smaller Euclidean constellation spacing. Simulated BER matched theoretical bounds, and perceptual metrics (PSNR, SSIM) confirmed the non-linear "cliff effect" inherent to visual data links.

6.2 Future Scope

Future work will focus on integrating Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) channel coding, extending simulations to frequency-selective channels using CP-OFDM, and conducting over-the-air validation on Software-Defined Radio (SDR) testbeds.
